title: Man who killed SQ officer in Louiseville began showing problems in 2012
article: The man who is alleged to have killed Sûreté du Québec Sgt. Maureen Breau in the line of duty in Louiseville suffered from mental health disorders for more than a decade and was considered to be "a significant risk" to public safety as recently as last year.

The details of Isaac Brouillard Lessard's mental health problems are detailed in a long series of decisions made since 2014 by the Commission d'examen des troubles mentaux, a tribunal composed of mental health experts who decide whether a person should remain detained at a mental health institution after they have been declared not criminally responsible in criminal cases.

According to the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes (BEI), Breau and a partner arrived at Brouillard Lessard's apartment, in the town 30 kilometres west of Trois-Rivières, Monday around 8:30 p.m. They were there to arrest the man on an allegation he had uttered threats.
"During the arrest, when the rights were being read, the individual took out a knife that he had nearby, then used it (to stab Breau)," the BEI wrote.

Another pair of SQ officers who arrived at the scene opened fire on Brouillard Lessard and he was killed. The owner of the apartment building told Le Nouvelliste, a newspaper based in Trois-Rivières, it was clear from the damage that several shots had been fired.
The SQ officer who accompanied Breau to make the arrest suffered injuries that were not considered to be life-threatening.
The BEI is in charge of the investigation into the police shooting.

Brouillard Lessard had been declared not criminally responsible in a series of criminal cases twice, in 2014 and 2018, at two different courthouses in Quebec. But his mental health problems first appeared two years earlier, on Oct. 21, 2012, when he was taken to an emergency room by paramedics on a request by police.
The police officers were attacked with a 20-pound dumbbell.

"The police officers also indicated he was a psychiatric patient in crisis, who said he is being persecuted by the Calabrian mafia. The next morning, the gentleman reported to the emergency doctor that he had watched a mafia film which, combined with the intake of alcohol and a family conflict, had led him to make comments which he said he no longer really remembers," the tribunal wrote in 2014 in its first decision concerning Brouillard Lessard. "However, he admitted to having consumed a bottle and a cup of wine as well as a joint. Urine drug tests came back positive for marijuana. The gentleman was then discharged."
Brouillard Lessard was returned to a mental health institution in 2013, on a request from his parents. He stayed there for roughly five weeks.
Later that same year, he told a mental health expert that he was taking medication that had been prescribed to him and that things were going well.

"He had just finished his seasonal job planting trees and was considering returning to school to finish high school. He remained mostly idle and smoked 4-5 joints of marijuana a day. He reported a good relationship with his father and had reconnected with his mother by phone, which was going well. He still occasionally thought about the traumatic events he believed he had experienced in the past, but did not worry too much about them," the tribunal wrote.

His plans to finish high school, while his was in his mid-20s, turned out to be short lived. He continued to do seasonal work and later claimed this caused problems when it came to taking his medication because he was dependent on his employer driving him back and forth to the remote locations where he would plant trees.

On March 10, 2014, Brouillard Lessard was declared not criminally responsible in two different cases where he was charged with uttering threats toward three of his relatives and, four months later, the mental health tribunal determined he should remain detained at an institution. The decision was based on a psychiatric diagnosis of delusional disorder, "but above all to his dependence on cannabis and his past alcohol abuse. He has narcissistic personality traits. According to the evidence, (Brouillard Lessard) has a fluctuating motivation towards treatment."

The following year, the tribunal determined his situation had improved to a point where he could be released from the hospital. He was required to live at a location assigned by the hospital and was required to follow any treatment prescribed to him.

In April 2018, Brouillard Lessard's doctors were informed that he had stopped taking his injectable medication. Six days later, he was taken to an emergency room again after he pulled a knife during an argument with his neighbours.

He was ordered to be hospitalized again in an effort to keep him on his medication but, in May 2018, he assaulted a psychiatrist, threatened another and assaulted two other people at the mental health institution where he was held. He was charged with the offences but was declared not criminally responsible at a courthouse in Shawinigan two months later, on July 18, 2018.
In the months that followed later that year, the Commission d'examen des troubles mentaux made two decisions to keep Brouillard Lessard detained at a mental health institution.

"He calls me a 'rotten doctor.' He affirms that I am 'judge and executioner.' He maintains that he is only aggressive towards psychiatrists who want to keep him in the hospital all his life and take away any chance of him working. He says he is not like other hospitalized people. He can work and have a life outside the hospital and he does not need more intensive psychiatric care," one psychiatrist informed the tribunal before it made one of the decisions in 2018.

He remained detained until 2020, when the tribunal decided: "Considering all of the evidence, the (tribunal) concludes that the accused still represents, because of his mental state, a significant risk to the safety of the public. However, (it) finds that public safety no longer dictates that the accused be kept in custody."
That decision was maintained again last year, even though Brouillard Lessard was still considered a significant risk to society.

Those decisions are similar to ones made by the same tribunal before Abdulla Shaikh, 26, killed three people, in Laval and the St-Laurent borough, before he was killed by police at a motel on Marcel-Laurin Blvd. in August last year.
